To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) ICTs can facilitate citizen communications in disaster contexts, and 2) ICTs can support the alignment of formal and informal response efforts.

public participation is an important aspect of ICT-enabled post-impact disaster communication, that the public can play a constructive role, and that the information pathways they use can be analyzed to understand their contributions.

public participation in disaster response is an emerging, computer-mediated arena for interaction that has implications both for informal and formal response, that persistent citizen communications are a form of interaction in that arena, and that these communications serve a variety of post-impact functions that are not well supported by current command-and-control models.
In summary, our research is concerned with
anticipating a future of crisis response that is more ICT-supported, more public, and more distributed.
the emerging information pathways of public participation and how they can be supported by ICT.
understanding the role of ICT in the emerging arena of public participation and the implications for formal response organizations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the future of ICT-supported citizen communication in disaster response is not yet clear, but it will be an important part of the response.
the future of citizen communications in disaster response is uncertain, and that the role of ICT is likely to increase.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ICT-supported public participation is a new and important arena for disaster research, and one that is likely to become increasingly important in the future.
the emerging information pathways are the result of a dynamic interplay between the information needs of citizens and the response organization, as well as the technological capabilities of ICT.

the future of public participation in crisis will be characterized by a more diverse set of information pathways, and that the challenge for response organizations is to develop a better understanding of the role of public participation in the overall response process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the future of ICT-supported citizen communication will likely involve the emergence of a new, hybrid form of public participation that combines formal and informal activities, and that is enabled by the Internet and other ICTs.

information science research needs to anticipate the emergence of a new, ICT-supported form of public participation in disaster contexts, and the implications this will have for the information needs of both citizens and response organizations.
information science researchers need to consider the role of public participation in disaster response as an emerging information environment, with its own information needs and practices.
